decks.title: Analysis of Financial Statements — Part 1: Meaning, Objectives, Tools, Limitations and Comparative Statements
goals: Explain the meaning, significance and objectives of financial statement analysis
Name the tools of analysis and state the limitations of analysis
Prepare a comparative statement of profit and loss with absolute and percentage changes
Prepare and read a comparative balance sheet

slides.heading: Analysis of Financial Statements
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what analysis is, who needs it, its **tools** and **limits**, and the **comparative statement**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: meaning and users, objectives, tools, limitations, then the comparative statement of profit and loss and the comparative balance sheet
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: A balance sheet and a statement of profit and loss are full of figures, but figures alone do not tell you whether a company is doing well. In this part we learn what financial analysis is, who uses it and why, which tools it uses and where it falls short. Then we prepare comparative statements, which set two years side by side.

slides.heading: What is financial statement analysis?
bullets: It **relates** figures to each other, to earlier years and to other firms.
The aim: judge **profitability, solvency and efficiency**, and support decisions.

nodes.label: Balance sheet and statement of profit and loss
Compare across years, firms or a base

visual.alt: Flow of financial statement analysis: the published statements are rearranged and grouped, compared across years, firms or a common base, interpreted for strengths and weaknesses, and used for decisions
visual.caption: Analysis turns finished statements into judgements.

slides.narration: Analysis starts after the accounts are finished. The analyst rearranges the items into meaningful groups, compares them with earlier years, with other firms or with a common base, and then interprets what the comparisons show. The result is a judgement about how profitable, how solvent and how efficient the company is, which people can act on.

slides.heading: Significance: who analyses, and why

rows: Where costs are rising, how efficiently resources are used, what to plan next
Profitability, growth and the safety of their money
Ability to pay within the credit period: short-term solvency
Ability to pay interest and repay over years: long-term solvency
Capacity to pay wages and bonus; job security

visual.alt: Table of users of financial analysis and what each wants to judge: management, investors, suppliers, lenders, employees and government

slides.narration: Many people read the same statements for different reasons. Management looks for rising costs and plans ahead. Investors want profit, growth and safety. Suppliers worry about being paid within the credit period, while lenders think about interest and repayment over many years. Employees think about wages and job security, and the government about tax and regulation.

slides.heading: Quick check: which is analysis?
slides.body_md: Pick the activity that analyses the statements rather than prepares them.
slides.narration: Ask whether the activity comes before the statements exist, or after them.

slides.heading: Objectives of analysis

rows: Is the company earning enough, and will it continue?
Can it pay its current liabilities on time?
Can it service and repay its long-term debt?
Better or worse than last year, and than other firms?
Why did profit or the financial position change?
What is likely next year, and what should be done?

visual.alt: Table of objectives of financial analysis with the question each answers: profitability, short-term and long-term solvency, comparison, reasons for change, forecasting

slides.narration: Analysis sets out to answer a few clear questions. Is the company earning enough, and will it continue? Can it pay what it owes soon, and what it owes over many years? Is it doing better than last year, and than its rivals? Why did profit change? And what is likely to happen next, so that plans can be made?

slides.heading: The tools of analysis
bullets: **Horizontal** analysis: the same item over time. **Vertical** analysis: items against a base within one year.

rows: Each item for two or more years, with absolute and percentage change
Each item as a percentage of a base of the same year
Inflows and outflows of cash by activity

visual.alt: Table of the four tools of financial analysis: comparative statements, common-size statements, ratio analysis and the cash flow statement, with what each shows
visual.caption: This chapter covers the first two tools.

slides.narration: There are four common tools. Comparative statements set two or more years side by side and show the change. Common-size statements express every item as a percentage of a base. Ratio analysis relates one item to another, and the cash flow statement shows where cash came from and went. This chapter covers the first two; ratios and cash flow follow in the next chapters.

slides.heading: Quick check: match the tools
slides.body_md: Match each tool with what it does.
slides.narration: Think of the key idea behind each tool: change over time, share of a base, a relationship, or the movement of cash.

slides.heading: Limitations of analysis

rows: The future may differ from the trend
Growth in rupees may only be inflation
Management quality, morale and reputation do not appear
Firms using different methods are hard to compare
The statements analysed may look better than reality
Two analysts may read the same figures differently

visual.alt: Table of limitations of financial analysis: past figures, inflation ignored, qualitative factors left out, different accounting policies, window dressing and the analyst’s judgement

slides.narration: Analysis is only as good as the figures it uses. Those figures describe the past and ignore inflation, so growth in rupees can mislead. Qualities such as good management never appear. Firms using different accounting methods are hard to compare, statements can be window-dressed, and in the end the analyst still has to use judgement.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: one figure is not enough
slides.body_md: An imagined company, **Sone Valley Biscuits Ltd**, Dehri, proudly reports that its profit after tax rose from ₹4,00,000 to ₹5,00,000. Its revenue from operations rose from ₹40,00,000 to ₹62,50,000. Did it really do better?

visual.alt: Table for worked example 1: revenue rose from 40,00,000 to 62,50,000, up 56.25 per cent; profit after tax rose from 4,00,000 to 5,00,000, up 25.00 per cent; but profit as a share of revenue fell from 10.00 to 8.00 per cent
visual.caption: Related figures tell a different story from a single figure.

slides.narration: Profit rose by twenty-five per cent, which sounds good. But revenue rose by fifty-six point two five per cent, much faster. As a share of revenue, profit fell from ten per cent to eight per cent. The company is bigger, but it keeps less of each rupee it earns. That is why analysts relate figures instead of reading one in isolation.

slides.heading: Quick check: what the figures missed
slides.body_md: A company with excellent figures loses its key team. Why did analysis not warn of it?
slides.narration: Can loyalty and skill be written in the books as an amount of money?

slides.heading: Comparative statements: the format
bullets: **Absolute change** = current year − previous year.
**Percentage change** = absolute change ÷ previous year × 100 (two decimals).

rows: Items in Schedule III order (profit and loss or balance sheet)
Amounts of the earlier year: the base
Current year − previous year (a fall in brackets)
Absolute change ÷ previous year × 100, to two decimals

visual.alt: Table of the five columns of a comparative statement: particulars, previous year, current year, absolute change, and percentage change on the previous year

slides.narration: A comparative statement has five columns: the particulars, the earlier year, the later year, the absolute change in rupees and the percentage change. The earlier year is always the base. A fall is shown in brackets or with a minus sign, and percentages are rounded to two decimal places.

slides.heading: Working out the changes
bullets: Work the **totals** from the rupee figures; never add or subtract percentages.
Show a fall in brackets: (25,000) and (12.50).

nodes.label: Write both years in Schedule III order
Check that the totals’ changes re-add

visual.alt: Flow of steps for a comparative statement: list both years in Schedule Three order, find the absolute change, divide by the previous year and multiply by one hundred, round to two decimals, and check that the changes of the totals re-add
visual.caption: Percentages of totals are worked out from the total amounts, never by adding percentages.

slides.narration: Work line by line. First write both years in Schedule Three order and finish every total. Then take the earlier figure away from the later one, divide by the earlier figure and multiply by one hundred. For a total, divide its own change by its own earlier amount; adding the percentages of the items would give the wrong answer.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: comparative statement of profit and loss
slides.body_md: An imagined textile company, **Shipra Fabrics Ltd**, Ujjain, pays tax at 30%. Its comparative statement of profit and loss:

rows: VI. Less: Tax (30% of profit before tax)

visual.alt: Comparative statement of profit and loss of Shipra Fabrics for two years: revenue up 30.00 per cent, total expenses up 31.89 per cent, profit after tax up 18.00 per cent
visual.caption: 27.88 and 31.89 are rounded to two decimals.

slides.narration: Revenue rose by thirty per cent, but total expenses rose faster, by thirty-one point eight nine per cent, because materials went up by thirty-seven point five per cent and finance costs by sixty per cent. Other income fell. So profit before tax, and profit after tax, rose by only eighteen per cent.

slides.heading: Worked example 2 (continued): reading the changes
bullets: Revenue up 30.00%, total expenses up 31.89%: costs are outrunning sales.
Profit after tax up only 18.00% (₹1,89,000).
Next step for management: find out why materials and finance costs rose so fast.

slides.heading: The comparative balance sheet

nodes.label: Both balance sheets, Schedule III order
Both totals change by the same amount

visual.alt: Flow for a comparative balance sheet: copy both balance sheets in Schedule Three order, find the change in each sub-head and its percentage on the earlier date, confirm both totals change by the same amount, then read sources against uses
visual.caption: A comparative balance sheet shows where new funds came from and where they went.

slides.narration: A comparative balance sheet works the same way. Write both balance sheets in Schedule Three order, find the change in each sub-head and its percentage on the earlier date, and check that the two totals changed by the same amount. Then read it as a story: where did new funds come from, and where were they used?

slides.heading: Worked example 3: comparative balance sheet
slides.body_md: An imagined maker of farm tools, **Zuari Agro Tools Ltd**, Margao, on 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2026:

rows: **(a) Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets**

visual.alt: Comparative balance sheet of Zuari Agro Tools on two dates; both totals rise by 8,50,000, that is 21.25 per cent

slides.narration: Both totals rise by rupees eight lakh fifty thousand, that is twenty-one point two five per cent. Share capital rose by a quarter and reserves by forty per cent, while trade payables fell by a quarter. On the assets side, property, plant and equipment rose by rupees six lakh.

slides.heading: Worked example 3 (continued): sources and uses
bullets: Long-term funds (owners and lenders) paid for the new fixed assets.
Trade payables were reduced: suppliers are being paid faster.

headers: Where the extra funds came from

visual.alt: Sources and uses for Zuari Agro Tools: shareholders' funds up 7,00,000, long-term borrowings up 2,00,000, current liabilities down 50,000; non-current assets up 6,50,000 and current assets up 2,00,000
visual.caption: Head totals are computed from the comparative balance sheet; both sides re-add.

slides.narration: Grouping the changes by head makes the picture clear. Owners put in rupees seven lakh more and lenders rupees two lakh, while current liabilities fell. Most of the money went into non-current assets. Financing long-lived assets with long-term funds is a sound policy.

slides.heading: Quick check: a percentage change
slides.body_md: Work it out to two decimals.
slides.narration: Divide the change by the earlier year, not the later one.

slides.heading: Quick check: assertion and reason
slides.body_md: Is a big percentage always a big amount?
slides.narration: Think of a small earlier figure. What does a large percentage of it amount to?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Relating figures to judge profitability, solvency and efficiency
Each reads the statements for its own decision
Past figures, inflation, no qualitative facts, policies, window dressing, judgement
Two years, absolute change, percentage change on the earlier year
Changes of totals re-add; both balance sheet totals change equally

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: meaning of analysis, users, tools, limitations, the comparative statement and its checks

slides.narration: To sum up: analysis relates figures to judge profitability, solvency and efficiency, and different users read it for different decisions. Its tools are comparative and common-size statements, ratios and the cash flow statement. It has limits, from inflation to accounting policies. A comparative statement shows two years with the absolute and percentage change, worked on the earlier year.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **heading** with the company name and both years or dates.
Keep the **Schedule III order** and the five columns; show falls in **brackets**.
Compute the percentage on the **previous year**, to **two decimals**.
Work the **totals from rupees**; never add the percentages of items.
For theory, give a **heading and a line** of explanation for each point.
slides.narration: In the exam, give a proper heading with the company name and both years. Keep the Schedule Three order and all five columns, and put a fall in brackets. Always divide by the previous year and round to two decimals. Work out the totals from the rupee figures. And for theory answers, give each point a heading and a line of explanation.

decks.title: Analysis of Financial Statements — Part 2: Common-size Statements and Interpretation
goals: Explain common-size statements and the base used in each
Prepare a common-size statement of profit and loss and a common-size balance sheet
Round to two decimals so that every column totals 100.00
Interpret comparative and common-size statements, including comparisons between firms

slides.heading: Common-size statements
slides.body_md: Part 2 — every item as a **percentage of a base**: the **common-size statement of profit and loss** and the **common-size balance sheet**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: meaning and base, common-size statement of profit and loss, common-size balance sheet, rounding so columns total one hundred, comparing firms and reading the results
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In part one we compared the same item across two years. Now we look down a single statement and ask what share each item takes of a base. These are common-size statements. We prepare them for the statement of profit and loss and the balance sheet, learn how to round so the columns total one hundred, and use them to compare firms of different sizes.

slides.heading: What is a common-size statement?
bullets: Also called **vertical** (static) analysis.
Shows the **make-up** of a statement and allows comparison of firms of different sizes.

rows: Common-size statement of profit and loss
Revenue from operations of the year
Balance sheet total (assets = equity and liabilities)

visual.alt: Table of the base for common-size statements: revenue from operations for the statement of profit and loss, and the balance sheet total for the balance sheet
visual.caption: Percentages are rounded to two decimals.

slides.narration: A common-size statement shows every item as a percentage of a common base. In the statement of profit and loss the base is revenue from operations; in the balance sheet it is the balance sheet total. Because everything becomes a share of one hundred, you can see the make-up of the statement and compare firms of any size.

slides.heading: Format: common-size statement of profit and loss
bullets: Other income is also a percentage **of revenue from operations**, so total income can exceed 100.

rows: above 100 if there is other income
V. Profit before Tax, VI. Tax, VII. Profit after Tax

visual.alt: Format of a common-size statement of profit and loss: amounts for both years and each line as a percentage of revenue from operations, with revenue at one hundred and total income above one hundred when there is other income

slides.narration: The statement keeps the rupee columns for both years and adds a percentage column for each. Revenue from operations is one hundred. Other income is shown as a percentage of revenue too, so total income goes above one hundred. Each expense, the total expenses, profit before tax, tax and profit after tax are all shares of revenue.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: common-size statement of profit and loss
slides.body_md: An imagined coffee processor, **Kabini Coffee Curing Ltd**, Mysuru, pays tax at 25%:

rows: VI. Less: Tax (25% of profit before tax)

visual.alt: Common-size statement of profit and loss of Kabini Coffee Curing: profit after tax 18.75 per cent of revenue in the earlier year and 16.50 per cent in the later year; materials 50.00 and 54.00 per cent
visual.caption: Base: revenue from operations of each year = 100.

slides.narration: Revenue is one hundred in each year. In the earlier year, total expenses take eighty per cent of revenue and profit after tax is eighteen point seven five per cent. In the later year, expenses take eighty-one per cent and profit after tax falls to sixteen point five per cent, even though profit in rupees went up.

slides.heading: Worked example 4 (continued): reading it
bullets: Materials: 50.00% → 54.00% of revenue — the main squeeze.
Employee benefits: 15.00% → 14.00% — slightly better.
Profit after tax: 18.75% → 16.50% — each rupee of sales now earns less.

slides.heading: Quick check: above one hundred
slides.body_md: Why can total income exceed 100 in a common-size statement of profit and loss?
slides.narration: Which single line is the base of one hundred?

slides.heading: The common-size balance sheet

nodes.label: Equity and liabilities: each sub-head ÷ total × 100

visual.alt: Flow for a common-size balance sheet: the balance sheet total is one hundred; each sub-head of equity and liabilities and of assets is divided by the total and multiplied by one hundred; each part adds to one hundred
visual.caption: One base for both parts, because the two totals are equal.

slides.narration: In a common-size balance sheet the base is the balance sheet total. Every sub-head of equity and liabilities, and every sub-head of assets, is divided by that total and multiplied by one hundred. Since the two parts have the same total, each part adds up to one hundred.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: common-size balance sheet
slides.body_md: An imagined handicraft company, **Barak Bamboo Crafts Ltd**, Silchar, on 31 March 2025 and 31 March 2026:

rows: **(a) Property, Plant and Equipment and Intangible Assets**

visual.alt: Common-size balance sheet of Barak Bamboo Crafts on two dates: share capital 50.00 and 55.00 per cent, long-term borrowings 20.00 and 12.50 per cent, property, plant and equipment 60.00 and 65.00 per cent
visual.caption: Base: the balance sheet total of each date = 100.

slides.narration: Share capital rose from fifty per cent to fifty-five per cent of the total, while long-term borrowings, unchanged in rupees, fell from twenty per cent to twelve point five per cent. On the assets side, property, plant and equipment rose to sixty-five per cent.

bullets: Owners now provide 75.00% of every rupee of funds, up from 65.00%.
Less reliance on borrowed funds: lower financial risk.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and kinds of financial analysis
sections.body_md:
**Analysis of financial statements** means studying the published statements critically: grouping related items, comparing them over time, with other firms or with a base, and interpreting the results to judge the **profitability, solvency and efficiency** of the business.

**Kinds of analysis**
- **Horizontal (dynamic):** the same item over two or more periods. Tool: comparative statements.
- **Vertical (static):** items of one period against a base of the same period. Tool: common-size statements.
- **Intra-firm** comparison: one firm against its own past. **Inter-firm** comparison: one firm against others in the industry.
- **External** analysis (by outsiders with published statements) and **internal** analysis (by management with full records).

key_terms.definition_md: Critical study of financial statements to judge profitability, solvency and efficiency.
Comparison of the same item across periods.
Comparison of items with a base within one period.

sections.heading: 2. Significance and objectives
sections.body_md:
**Significance (users):** management (planning, cost control, efficiency); investors (profitability, growth, safety); trade payables (payment within the credit period); lenders and debenture holders (interest and repayment over years); employees and unions (wages, bonus, job security); government and researchers (tax, regulation, industry studies).

**Objectives**
1. Assess profitability and earning capacity.
2. Assess short-term solvency (liquidity).
3. Assess long-term solvency.
4. Make intra-firm and inter-firm comparisons.
5. Find the reasons for changes in profit and financial position.
6. Help forecasting, budgeting and planning.

sections.heading: 3. Tools of analysis
sections.body_md:
- **Comparative statements:** two or more years side by side with absolute and percentage changes.
- **Common-size statements:** every item as a percentage of a common base of the same period.
- **Ratio analysis:** relationships between related items (Chapter 10).
- **Cash flow statement:** inflows and outflows of cash from operating, investing and financing activities (Chapter 11).

sections.heading: 4. Limitations of analysis
sections.body_md:
- **Historical:** based on past figures; the future may be different.
- **Price-level changes ignored:** figures of different years are compared in rupees of different value.
- **Qualitative aspects ignored:** quality of management, industrial relations, reputation.
- **Different accounting policies:** methods of depreciation and inventory valuation differ between firms, which spoils inter-firm comparison.
- **Window dressing:** statements may present a better picture than the real one.
- **Analyst’s bias and skill:** analysis indicates symptoms; diagnosis needs judgement.

A single figure means little: relate it to others (worked example 1).

**Columns:** Particulars | previous year (₹) | current year (₹) | absolute change (₹) | percentage change (%).

**Formulas**

Expenses (cost of materials consumed, purchases of stock-in-trade, change in inventories, employee benefits, finance costs, depreciation and amortisation, other expenses) and total expenses; V. Profit before tax; VI. Tax; VII. Profit after tax.

sections.heading: 8. Interpreting comparative and common-size statements
sections.body_md:
- Compare the **growth of each expense** with the growth of revenue: costs growing faster squeeze profit.
- Track the **share** of each cost in revenue: a rising materials share means higher input costs or prices not raised.
- Watch **finance costs** and the **share of borrowings**: more debt, more risk.
- Check how **fixed assets** were financed: long-term funds are the sound source.
- Remember that a falling **share** does not mean a falling **amount**, and a large **percentage** change may be a small **rupee** change.
- Use **both** tools: comparative shows speed of change; common-size shows structure.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Dividing the change by the **current** year instead of the previous year.
- Adding the percentage changes of items to get the percentage change of a total.
- Using **total income** as the base of a common-size statement of profit and loss (the base is revenue from operations).
- Leaving a common-size balance sheet column at 99.99 or 100.01 without adjusting and noting it.
- Forgetting brackets for a fall, or forgetting the heading with both years.
- In interpretation, describing the numbers without giving the **reason** and the **effect**.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a concept, a base, a single percentage, or an assertion-reason item.
- 3 marks: three objectives or limitations; a short comparative or common-size statement (format, absolute change, percentages).
- 4 marks: a full comparative or common-size statement of profit and loss or balance sheet.
- 6 marks: a statement with interpretation, or theory with meaning, objectives and limitations.

questions.stem_md: Nisha, a commerce student, has the balance sheets and statements of profit and loss of an imagined company for two years. Which activity of hers is the analysis of financial statements?

options.text_md: Recording the transactions of the year in the journal and posting them to the ledger
Relating the figures to each other and across the years to judge the profitability and financial strength of the company
Checking the vouchers behind every entry, as an auditor does
Preparing the trial balance from the ledger balances

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Relating the figures to each other and across the years to judge the profitability and financial strength of the company. Analysis begins where the accounts end: it takes the finished statements, sets items against each other and against earlier years, and draws conclusions. Recording, posting, vouching and the trial balance all come before the statements exist.

questions.stem_md: A bank is considering a seven-year term loan to an imagined company, Lohit Tea Estates Ltd, Dibrugarh. Through financial analysis, the bank is chiefly trying to judge

options.text_md: the market price of the company's shares next month
how many workers the company employs on each tea estate
whether the directors are related to each other
the company's long-term solvency: whether it can pay interest regularly and repay the loan when due

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** the company's long-term solvency: whether it can pay interest regularly and repay the loan when due. A long-term lender is repaid over several years, so it studies the capital structure, the profit available to cover interest and the stability of earnings.

questions.stem_md: An analyst places the financial statements of two imagined cement makers, Arpa Cement Ltd and Sankh Cement Ltd, side by side for the same year to see which uses its resources better. This is an example of

options.text_md: inter-firm comparison
intra-firm comparison
a cash flow analysis
an audit of the two companies

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** inter-firm comparison. Comparing different firms for the same period is inter-firm comparison; comparing one firm with itself over several periods is intra-firm (time series) comparison.

questions.stem_md: Analysing the statements of a single year by expressing each item as a percentage of a common base is known as

options.text_md: horizontal analysis
trend forecasting
vertical analysis
internal audit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** vertical analysis. Vertical (static) analysis studies the relationship of items within one period; common-size statements are its usual form.

questions.stem_md: Comparative statements are said to be a form of horizontal analysis because

options.text_md: they express every item as a percentage of a single base figure of one year
they are always prepared in the horizontal (T-shaped) form of the balance sheet
they compare the same item across two or more accounting periods
they are prepared only by analysts outside the company

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** they compare the same item across two or more accounting periods. The reader moves across the columns, from one year to the next, for each item; that movement over time is what "horizontal" refers to, not the shape of the statement.

questions.stem_md: Two imagined footwear makers, Palar Leather Ltd and Ponnaiyar Shoes Ltd, value their closing inventory by different acceptable methods and charge depreciation at different rates. An analyst comparing their profit margins should remember that

options.text_md: differences in accounting policies can make an inter-firm comparison misleading
the comparison is impossible, because only firms of the same size can be compared
analysis automatically removes the effect of different accounting policies
inventory and depreciation never affect the profit of a company

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** differences in accounting policies can make an inter-firm comparison misleading. The same transactions can produce different profits under different policies, so part of the gap between the two margins may come from the methods, not from performance.

questions.stem_md: The comparative statements of an imagined software company, Kopai Digital Ltd, show rising revenue and profit. Shortly afterwards, its entire product design team resigns, which hurts the company badly. The analysis failed to warn of this because

options.text_md: comparative statements cannot be prepared for software companies
the analyst should have used a common-size balance sheet instead
revenue and profit are never relevant to a software company
financial analysis ignores qualitative factors that cannot be expressed in money

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** financial analysis ignores qualitative factors that cannot be expressed in money. The skill and loyalty of a team carry no rupee value in the books, so no tool built on the financial statements can pick them up.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following is NOT a tool of analysis of financial statements?

options.text_md: Common-size statements
Bank reconciliation statement
Ratio analysis
Cash flow statement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Bank reconciliation statement. A bank reconciliation explains the gap between the cash book and the pass book; it is a bookkeeping check, not a method of analysing the published statements.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The results of financial analysis must be interpreted with care before a decision is taken.

**Reason (R):** Analysis only points out symptoms, such as a falling margin; finding the cause needs further enquiry and judgement.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. A changed figure tells the analyst where to look, not why it changed, and that is exactly why interpretation needs care; R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Inter-firm comparison through financial analysis may be misleading when the firms follow different accounting policies.

**Reason (R):** Every company is required by law to use the same method of depreciation and of valuing inventory.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: companies may choose among accepted methods for depreciation and inventory, and that freedom is the very reason comparisons between firms can mislead.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Because it compares figures of several years, financial analysis automatically corrects for changes in the price level.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Figures of different years are compared at their book amounts. A rise in rupees may only reflect inflation, which the analyst has to allow for separately.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Analysis of financial statements is useful to the management of a company as well as to outsiders such as lenders and investors.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Management uses it for planning and control, while lenders, investors, suppliers and the government use it for their own decisions.

questions.stem_md: Studying how each item of the financial statements has moved from one year to the next is called ___ analysis.
questions.solution_md: Horizontal (dynamic) analysis follows each item over time; comparative statements are its usual tool.

questions.stem_md: Match each tool of financial analysis in column A with what it does in column B.

options.text_md: Comparative statements
Common-size statements
Ratio analysis
Cash flow statement

match_right.text_md: Show each item as a percentage of a common base of the same year
Explains the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents during a period
Show each item for two or more years with its absolute and percentage change
Relates one item to another, such as current assets to current liabilities

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Change over years, share of a base, the relation between two items, and the movement of cash are the four ideas behind the four tools.

questions.stem_md: Four people are studying the statements of an imagined company, Shivnath Rice Mills Ltd. Match the question each one is asking (column A) with the purpose of analysis it serves (column B).

options.text_md: A paddy supplier: "Will my bills be paid within sixty days?"
A debenture holder: "Will interest keep coming for the next eight years?"
A shareholder: "Is the company earning more on every rupee of sales than before?"
The managing director: "Are we doing better or worse than other rice mills?"

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(q), (b)–(s), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Each question names a period or a comparison: weeks point to liquidity, years to solvency, margins to profitability, and other mills to comparison between firms.

questions.stem_md: State any three objectives of analysing the financial statements of a company.
questions.solution_md: Any three distinct objectives, each with a line on what the analyst learns.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **To judge profitability and earning capacity:** whether the company earns an adequate profit on its revenue and on the funds employed, and whether that profit is likely to continue.
2. **To assess solvency:** short-term (can current liabilities be met from current assets?) and long-term (can interest be paid and loans repaid?).
3. **To make comparisons:** with the company's own earlier years (intra-firm) and with other firms in the industry (inter-firm), so that strengths and weak spots stand out.
4. *(Also accepted)* To find the reasons for changes in profit or financial position; to judge how efficiently management has used the resources; to help forecast future results and plan.

questions.stem_md: Ritu, a junior analyst, has prepared comparative and common-size statements of an imagined company, Pranhita Pulses Ltd, and tells her manager, "The numbers say it all; we need nothing else to recommend the shares." State three limitations of financial analysis that her manager should point out to her.
questions.solution_md: Three limitations, each tied to why the numbers cannot be the whole basis for the recommendation.

answer.model_answer_md:
- **It works on past figures.** The statements she analysed describe last year; an investment decision depends on future results, which have to be judged separately.
- **Price changes are ignored.** Rupee figures of different years are compared as they stand, so part of any growth may be inflation, and assets bought long ago appear at old costs.
- **Non-money factors are left out.** The quality of management, labour relations or a new competitor do not appear in the statements, though they can change the outlook of a pulse processor completely.
- *(Also accepted)* The figures depend on accounting policies and estimates, and may be window-dressed; analysis shows symptoms, not causes, and still needs the analyst's judgement.

questions.stem_md: An imagined company, Hasdeo Paper Board Ltd, Korba, is studied by (i) its finance manager, (ii) a trade union negotiating wages, and (iii) a supplier of wood pulp who gives ninety days of credit. Explain how financial analysis is significant to each of them.
questions.solution_md: For each party, name the decision first and then the part of the analysis that serves it.

answer.model_answer_md:
- **(i) Finance manager:** uses the analysis to see which costs are rising faster than revenue, whether the capital structure is sound and where funds are tied up, and so plans borrowing, cost control and investment.
- **(ii) Trade union:** studies the trend of profit and of employee benefits expense as a share of revenue to argue what wage rise or bonus the company can afford, and judges how secure the jobs are.
- **(iii) Wood pulp supplier:** looks at short-term solvency, current assets against current liabilities and the cash position, to decide whether the ninety days of credit is safe and how much to supply.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between horizontal analysis and vertical analysis of financial statements on any three bases.
questions.solution_md: Three bases, each stated for both kinds of analysis.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Basis | Horizontal analysis | Vertical analysis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Period covered | Two or more years of the same firm | One year (or one statement) at a time |
| What is compared | The same item across years: absolute and percentage change | Each item with a base of the same year, such as revenue from operations or the balance sheet total |
| Usual tool | Comparative statements | Common-size statements |
| Also called | Dynamic analysis | Static analysis |

questions.stem_md: Name and briefly explain the four tools commonly used to analyse the financial statements of a company.
questions.solution_md: Four tools, each with what it shows; a definition without its purpose earns half the mark.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Comparative statements:** the statement of profit and loss or the balance sheet of two or more years placed side by side, with the absolute change in each item and the change as a percentage of the earlier year. They show the direction and size of change (horizontal analysis).
2. **Common-size statements:** every item of a statement expressed as a percentage of a common base, revenue from operations for the statement of profit and loss and the balance sheet total for the balance sheet. They show the make-up of a statement and let firms of different sizes be compared (vertical analysis).
3. **Ratio analysis:** relationships between two related figures, such as current assets to current liabilities or profit to revenue, used to judge liquidity, solvency, activity and profitability.
4. **Cash flow statement:** a statement of the inflows and outflows of cash and cash equivalents from operating, investing and financing activities, showing where cash came from and how it was used.

questions.stem_md: (a) What is meant by analysis of financial statements? (b) Explain any three objectives of such analysis. (c) State any two of its limitations.
questions.solution_md: Give the meaning in one or two sentences, three objectives with explanation and two limitations.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Meaning.** Analysis of financial statements is the systematic study of the balance sheet and the statement of profit and loss of an enterprise, in which related items are grouped, compared over time or with other firms, and set against each other, so as to judge its profitability, solvency and efficiency and to support decisions.

**(b) Objectives (any three).**
1. To assess the earning capacity: how much profit is earned on revenue and on capital, and how it is changing.
2. To judge solvency: the ability to meet short-term obligations and to service and repay long-term debt.
3. To compare performance with earlier years and with similar firms, to locate strengths and weaknesses.
4. *(Also accepted)* To understand why profit or the financial position changed; to forecast and plan; to judge the efficiency of management.

**(c) Limitations (any two).**
- Analysis rests on historical, unadjusted figures, so changes in the price level distort comparisons between years.
- Qualitative factors are ignored, and different accounting policies or window dressing can make the figures, and so the analysis, misleading.

questions.stem_md: In a comparative statement, the percentage change in an item is calculated on

options.text_md: the amount of the earlier (base) year
the amount of the current year
the total of the balance sheet
revenue from operations of the current year

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** the amount of the earlier (base) year. Percentage change = absolute change ÷ earlier-year amount × 100, so the earlier year is the base.

questions.stem_md: Trade receivables of an imagined company, Mula Seeds Ltd, were ₹2,40,000 on 31 March 2025 and ₹3,00,000 on 31 March 2026. In its comparative balance sheet, the percentage change in trade receivables is
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** 25.00%. Change = 3,00,000 − 2,40,000 = 60,000; 60,000 ÷ 2,40,000 × 100 = 25.00%. Dividing by the later figure is the usual slip.

questions.stem_md: Other income of an imagined company, Koyna Plastics Ltd, was ₹1,60,000 in 2024-25 and ₹1,20,000 in 2025-26. In the comparative statement of profit and loss, the absolute and percentage change are shown as

options.text_md: 40,000 and 25.00, an increase
(40,000) and (33.33), a decrease
(40,000) and (25.00), a decrease
40,000 and 33.33, an increase

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** (40,000) and (25.00), a decrease. Change = 1,20,000 − 1,60,000 = −40,000, and −40,000 ÷ 1,60,000 × 100 = −25.00%. A fall is shown in brackets (or with a minus sign), and the base is still the earlier year.

questions.stem_md: The comparative statement of profit and loss of an imagined company shows that revenue from operations rose by 20% while total expenses rose by 28%. The company has no other income and earned a profit in both years. Its profit before tax has therefore

options.text_md: grown by exactly 20%
grown by more than 28%
grown by 8%, the difference between the two rates
grown by less than 20%, and may even have fallen

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** grown by less than 20%, and may even have fallen. Profit is what is left of revenue after expenses. When expenses grow faster than revenue, the leftover grows more slowly than revenue, and if the expense base is large it can shrink; subtracting one growth rate from the other is not a valid shortcut.

questions.stem_md: In a comparative balance sheet, the absolute change in total equity and liabilities between the two dates is always equal to

options.text_md: the absolute change in share capital
the profit after tax of the later year
